summary: This benchmark evaluates cross-model causal activation transplantation between a frozen Qwen2.5-Coder-7B donor and a frozen Qwen2.5-72B host on a controlled Python variable-reading task. The experimental design is methodologically sound, employing rigorous control conditions (unused-variable edits, norm-matched orthogonal vectors, and full-state swaps) along with exact hardware, software, and checkpoint documentation.
strengths: Methodologically sound interventional design incorporating proper negative controls, including norm-matched orthogonal perturbations and edits to unused assignment sites.
Comprehensive documentation of hardware configuration, software package versions, peak memory consumption, and commit-pinned model checkpoints.
Clear quantitative evaluation using full-vocabulary rank criteria without permissive top-k slack, supported by 5,000-draw bootstrap confidence intervals.
Directly builds upon and extends established causal abstraction and model stitching frameworks to large-scale (72B) open weights.
weaknesses: The evaluation scope is restricted to synthetic, single-digit Python arithmetic tasks with rigid prompt structures rather than diverse reasoning benchmarks.
The intervention is evaluated at only a single layer boundary (donor layer 6 to host layer 17) rather than systematically mapping layer-to-layer transferability.
As acknowledged by the author, token order and variable position remain coupled, leaving the asymmetric difficulty of the first assignment unexplained.
suggestions: Expand evaluation beyond single-digit integer assignments to multi-digit arithmetic, string variables, or multi-step logic to test generalizability.
Conduct a layer-wise intervention grid search across donor and host transformer blocks to characterize where transfer succeeds or degrades.
Counterbalance variable assignment ordering in the prompt template to eliminate position bias as a confounding factor.
